### Observed differences

- **A12:** before, its work was spread across about 44 distinct resource codes, with one code (User_1) handling about 40 in 100 assignments; in the later window, every one of about 190 observed assignments went to a single code (User_36), and the concentration index rose from about 0.18 to 1.0. [ASSIGN003, CONC001]
- **A13, A14 and A17:** the share of assignments handled by User_71 rose from about 5–6 in 100 to about 24–25 in 100, overtaking the code that had led these activities before (about 11–13 in 100, now outside the top shares); assignment volumes stayed similar (about 340 observations per window for A13/A14, about 305–310 for A17). [ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- **A01, A03 and A22:** the mix of codes holding the top assignment shares changed — several codes that each held roughly 3–12 in 100 of assignments before dropped out of the top shares, replaced by other codes at roughly 4–8 in 100 after, while the aggregated remaining share stayed around 38–48 in 100 in both windows. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN007]
- **Timing:** for the A03/A13 activity pair, the elapsed time between consecutive completions fell from a median of about 168 hours to about 66 hours (mean about 167 to about 72 hours), with the middle 50% of gaps narrowing from about 115–195 hours to about 48–77 hours; the pair was observed 58 times before and 80 times after, out of 200 traces in each window. [TWAIT001]
- Screening context: 8 resource items and 1 time item qualified, against about 0.005 and 0.02 expected by chance in those families; no control-flow item qualified (0 against about 0.18). [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that the allocation of work to resources changed between the windows. A12 moved from distributed handling across many codes, led by User_1 with about 40 in 100 assignments, to exclusive handling by User_36; on A13, A14 and A17, assignments shifted strongly toward User_71 (from about 5–6 in 100 to about 24–25 in 100) while the previously leading code fell out of the top shares; and on A01, A03 and A22 a recurring set of codes took over the top assignment shares from a different set that had held them. The change is in who is assigned rather than in whether the activities run: assignment volumes were broadly similar across windows (A12 about 200 vs 190, A13/A14 about 343 vs 342, A17 about 305 vs 310, A22 about 121 vs 138 observations), and no control-flow item qualified. The resource family produced 8 items against about 0.005 expected without change, so chance cannot account for the family as a whole, and every item exceeds about 9995 of 10000 random re-splits. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so the evidence cannot distinguish a change in assignment behaviour from a change in the composition of the resource pool; A12's result is described by two indicators of the same underlying assignments, and A13 and A14 show identical profiles in both windows, so these items are not independent confirmations. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001, screening]

Other differences: The elapsed time between consecutive completions for the A03/A13 pair fell by roughly 100 hours at the median (about 168 to about 66 hours). Because the time family produced only 1 item against about 0.02 expected by chance, this single result is within what an unchanged process typically yields at these thresholds; it remains a possible timing change that the screening count does not support. [TWAIT001, screening]
